title: wkappbot exec --keystrokes-file: live ConPTY relay + T0-T3 ladder
desc: wkappbot exec's built-in ConPTY keystrokes-file feature (RunCommand.Pty.cs), PseudoConsoleRunner gotchas, the standardized non-hardcoded escalation design, and the zombie-process fix.
steps: WHAT: wkappbot exec <target> --keystrokes-file <path> drives a target through a real Windows ConPTY, live-polling the given file every 300ms (FileStream+FileShare.ReadWrite+lastReadPosition delta-read) and injecting newly appended bytes into the child's stdin for the life of the session -- lets a caller answer TUI prompts that appear mid-run, not just at launch.

IMPL: RunCommand.Pty.cs RunExecPtyBranch wires this into PseudoConsoleRunner.Run(..., mirrorToTerminal: true, useFixedLargeSize: keystrokesFile != null). useFixedLargeSize=true fixes ConPTY size at 220x50 and disables both the resize-watcher thread and the competing RelayInput(Console.ReadKey) thread, since automation callers need neither.

GOTCHA (mirror channel): mirrorToTerminal and process-level stdout-redirect capture share the SAME Console.Out channel -- there is no separate internal buffer. A --no-mirror flag was prototyped then fully reverted after live testing proved it breaks automation capture entirely (0 bytes captured). Do not re-add --no-mirror without first building a genuinely separate capture buffer.

GOTCHA (drain-or-stall): the child's stdout MUST be drained continuously via BaseStream.CopyToAsync() started immediately after Process.Start() -- sleeping/polling then reading at the end causes OS pipe-buffer backpressure that silently stalls the whole ConPTY session. This caused 6 consecutive false stuck-bug reports in one session before being traced to the TEST HARNESS itself, not the feature.

STANDARDIZED ESCALATION LADDER (design target, not yet wired into RunCommand.Pty.cs) for driving an arbitrary target with zero per-app hardcoding -- T0 subsystem check (IsConsoleSubsystemExe, PE header Subsystem field): GUI-subsystem apps have no stdin/stdout interaction surface at all, route to a11y/UIA instead of any pipe/ConPTY attempt. T1 plain pipe first (cheapest; most non-interactive-capable CLIs, e.g. codex exec, read stdin fine with zero ConPTY -- but always explicitly close/EOF the child's stdin, codex exec itself hangs forever on a dangling open non-tty pipe, see github.com/openai/codex issues 27019/20919). T2 if T1 shows a GENERIC failure signal (fast exit, near-zero stdout, nonzero exit code -- never string-match one app's specific error text) escalate to ConPTY + --keystrokes-file, which is what makes ConPTY-sensitive TUIs like agy.exe actually render. T3 if ConPTY ALSO shows the same generic failure signal, this exact commandline cannot be driven via any pipe/ConPTY mechanism -- report cleanly and stop; never hardcode a per-app fallback command inside exec's core logic (that knowledge belongs to the caller, not the bridge).

VERIFIED MECHANISM (direct probe): a child spawned under a genuine ConPTY (CreatePseudoConsole + PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_PSEUDOCONSOLE, no STARTF_USESTDHANDLES) still sees its own GetStdHandle(STD_INPUT_HANDLE)/STDOUT as FILE_TYPE_PIPE with GetConsoleMode failing (err=6 ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE) -- IDENTICAL to a plain redirected pipe with no ConPTY at all. Confirmed via a standalone GetFileType/GetConsoleMode probe run both ways side by side. This is the underlying mechanism behind the codex-cannot-be-driven finding in wkstdpty-shared-pty-bridge -- do not re-run that investigation, it is closed.

ZOMBIE FIX: IocpPipeRelay.cs ties Core's process lifetime to the Launcher's own OS process handle via CreateJobObjectW+JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE+AssignProcessToJobObject (TieCoreToLauncherLifetime in Program.PInvoke.cs), so an external kill of the Launcher no longer leaves orphaned wkappbot exec agy.exe zombies for hours. Root cause was two layers: a dead --exit-event wiring bug (cosmetic) AND wktest-build.sh silently deploying the Launcher from the WRONG sibling repo with the wrong TFM folder name, so 3+ earlier fix attempts never reached the actually-running binary -- always verify via the deployed exe's file timestamp before declaring a deploy-dependent fix done.

RECOVERY NOTE (2026-07-23): this skill was accidentally deleted mid-session by a stray rm -rf on a scratch skills/ fork directory that was wrongly assumed already-synced-to-HQ when it was not -- recreated identically from the orchestrating session's own conversation record. Lesson: never rm -rf a skill fork directory without first confirming via wkappbot skill read <id> that the content is independently retrievable from HQ.

OUTPUT-AS-INTERCEPT: what --on-match makes possible, and where it must NOT be trusted (design note 2026-07-23). Until now a CLI could only be governed if IT supported a PreToolUse hook -- which is exactly why agy scores NOT-GATED (its native C++ permission engine sees the call first) and why codex cannot be hooked at all. A live output matcher inverts that: the child's own SCREEN becomes the interception point, so a hookless CLI can be wrapped from OUTSIDE. Answering a prompt with a refusal is functionally a Stop, and a rule can also drive recovery ('context low' -> /compact). THE HARD LIMIT, which must never be blurred: this is ADVISORY, not enforcement. It is (1) POST-DECISION -- the model already chose the action and the CLI already rendered the prompt; we only answer it, (2) DEFEATABLE -- a changed prompt string, a locale change, an unexpected ANSI form, or a silently auto-granted call produces NO output to match and the rule never fires, and (3) FAIL-OPEN by nature -- no match means no action, whereas a real gate denies what it cannot prove safe. Therefore: NEVER present --on-match coverage as harness coverage, never let it satisfy the 99 test C2 criterion (hook fires >= tool calls), and never point it at our OWN gates to auto-answer them -- a gate that answers itself has stopped being a gate. Correct use: driving a FOREIGN CLI's prompts unattended, with explicit per-rule intent and a fire cap. Cross: agy-99-harness-connection-e2e-test (the NOT-GATED verdict this does NOT fix), agy-harness-popup-deadlock-ref (the ANSI-decoder trap that makes naive matching silently miss).

SPEC: --on-match reactive responder + --trim noise normalisation (authored 2026-07-23, implementation in flight). SYNTAX: --on-match "<REGEX>=><SEQ>" repeatable, rules evaluated in the order given, first match wins per scan; --trim "<REGEX>" deletes and --trim "<REGEX>=><replacement>" substitutes, also repeatable. Both split on the FIRST => so a regex may contain >. SEQ reuses the EXACT --exit-input token grammar (ESC, ENTER=CR 0x0D, TAB, CTRL+A..Z arithmetic, ALT+key, CSI keys, star-N repetition, WAIT:ms, hex escapes, literals) -- one parser, never a second. PIPELINE ORDER, the part that must not be reordered: raw bytes -> decode -> ANSI strip -> trim rules in caller order -> rolling multi-KB window -> on-match evaluation. Trims change only what is MATCHED, never what is SENT. Rolling window (not per-read-chunk) because a prompt can split across reads; after a rule fires, drop the matched region and apply a per-rule cooldown (default 750ms) so the same still-visible text does not refire. STREAM SCOPE: under ConPTY the child's stdout and stderr are MULTIPLEXED into one pseudo-console stream -- the matcher inherently sees both and they CANNOT be told apart, so no per-stream filter option exists for that path and the help must say so rather than fake a separation; the plain-pipe path has genuinely separate handles and watches both, but never at the cost of the drain-or-stall rule (a stalled pipe is a hang, worse than an unsplit stream). EVIDENCE INTEGRITY: trims apply to the match window ONLY -- the saved transcript stays RAW unless --trim-log is passed explicitly (default off). This is not a preference: the raw transcript is what proved what a run actually did when an agent report was wrong. SAFETY RAILS: per-rule fire cap default 100 via --on-match-max, then stop firing and log loudly (an unbounded responder against a looping prompt is an infinite loop that looks like progress); NO blanket auto-approve mode, ever -- every rule is caller-authored and a deny rule is as valid as an allow rule; log every fire to stderr because silent automation is unauditable; an unparseable rule ABORTS at startup naming it, because a silently-dropped rule is indistinguishable from one that matched nothing. NO PRESETS until real usage shows which noise repeats. VERIFICATION that actually proves something: for trim, show the rule NOT firing on noise-broken text and then firing with the trim added -- the failing half is the proof; for on-match, drive a target that genuinely blocks (a Read-Host loop), never one that would finish anyway. Limits of the whole mechanism: see the OUTPUT-AS-INTERCEPT step -- advisory, post-decision, fail-open, never harness coverage.

TODO: 2026-07-23 HOLD THE ConPTY INPUT SIDE OPEN FOR THE CHILD'S LIFETIME (root-cause fix, spec). SYMPTOM: every well-behaved console app sees stdin EOF the instant it starts under 'wkappbot exec', so it cannot block for input at all. Measured: choice.exe -- the Windows built-in whose entire purpose is to block on a keypress -- prints 'Continue [Y,N]?' then exits code=255 in ~1.1s; the same happens WITH --keys pointing at a file (1.2s), so supplying a keystrokes file does not hold the channel open; PowerShell Read-Host returns an EMPTY STRING instead of blocking; [Console]::ReadKey() throws 'Cannot be called when input is redirected'. WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE SYMPTOM: --keys and --reply can only ever drive a target that IGNORES EOF and runs its own read loop -- which is exactly and only what agy.exe does. The feature appearing to work is therefore an ACCIDENT of one target's behaviour, not a contract, and no certified blocking target can exist to verify it (three verification attempts produced false PASSes because of this). FIX: keep the write end of the pseudo-console INPUT pipe open for as long as the child lives -- create it, hand the read end to the child, and hold our write handle rather than closing it after the initial write; close it only at teardown or when the caller explicitly asks for EOF. Consider an explicit --stdin-eof flag for the rare caller that genuinely wants the child to see EOF immediately. VERIFY, in this order and no other: (1) WITHOUT the fix, choice.exe exits 255 in about a second -- record that baseline; (2) WITH the fix, the same command BLOCKS until the timeout; (3) only then add --reply and require the '[EXEC:PTY] reply rule#N fired' log line, not merely the downstream outcome, because the outcome alone is what produced every earlier false PASS. Files: PseudoConsoleRunner.cs (input handle lifetime) and RunCommand.Pty.cs (the exec branch that wires it).

CORRECTION 2026-07-23 -- the stdin-EOF diagnosis in step 11 is WRONG; the measured cause is NO USABLE CONSOLE in the child. Measured from inside the child: GetStdHandle(STD_INPUT) SUCCEEDS and GetFileType reports FILE_TYPE_CHAR, but GetConsoleMode, GetNumberOfConsoleInputEvents and GetConsoleScreenBufferInfo ALL fail with error 6 ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE. So the handle exists and looks like a character device while the legacy console API surface is absent -- which is exactly why choice.exe (which reads via ReadConsoleInput) cannot work. HOW THE EARLIER DIAGNOSIS FOOLED US: choice exits 255 printing 'The file is either empty or does not contain the valid choices', which reads like an argument error and was inferred to be an EOF-on-stdin symptom. It is neither: that message is what choice emits whenever its CONSOLE is unavailable. Proven by reproducing it with NO ConPTY involved at all -- Start-Process choice.exe with stdout/stderr redirected fails identically, while the same command in a real console prompts correctly and honours /T /D with rc=1. TWO REUSABLE LESSONS. (1) choice.exe is a CONSOLE-PRESENCE DETECTOR, not a blocking target: it never blocks once redirected, so it can prove whether a child has a real console but can never prove a reply/keystroke feature works. (2) A CONTROL RUN MUST BE GENUINELY UNCONTROLLED -- the measurement round's 'normal terminal' baseline was itself launched through a redirected harness context, so it showed the SAME failures as the patient and nearly buried the finding; a control captured through the same plumbing as the patient is not a control. NEXT INVESTIGATION, in this order: confirm whether the exec path ACTUALLY takes the ConPTY branch (the banner prints '[EXEC:PTY] Launching (ConPTY)' while the child behaves like a redirected-pipe child), and whether the child is attached to the pseudoconsole via PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_PSEUDOCONSOLE with NO STARTF_USESTDHANDLES override -- setting both is the classic mistake that yields exactly this symptom.

MIGRATED to wkexec-conpty-keystrokes-ladder-ref (2026-07-23): the full correction chain -- both wrong diagnoses, the two measurement confounds, and the two real bugs found -- now lives in that ref tier. Summary kept here: Ground truth, measured with an ABSOLUTE target path: 'exec C:/Windows/System32/cmd.exe /c "mode con"' takes the ConPTY branch and the child prints 'Status for device CON: Lines 30, Columns 120' -- the child HAS a real console, so ConPTY attachment is healthy and the earlier ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE readings came from a broken P/Invoke probe, not from the runtime. THE ACTUAL BUG: exec's own flags are not stripped from the child command line when they follow the target. The launch banner shows it verbatim -- 'Launching (ConPTY): choice.exe /C YN /M Continue --keys D:/...y-keys.txt' -- so choice received '--keys <path>' as bogus choice arguments and exited 255 with its misleading 'file is either empty or does not contain the valid choices'. powershell hid this for weeks because it silently ignores surplus arguments. TWO CONFOUNDS THAT WASTED THREE ROUNDS, both worth a permanent reflex: (1) MSYS PATH CONVERSION -- from Git-Bash, '/c' is rewritten to 'C:/' before wkappbot ever sees it, so ANY Windows-style switch must be run with MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 or the test measures something else entirely; (2) SHIM HIJACK -- 'exec cmd' resolves to bin/cmd.CMD (a wkwrap shim), which takes the ad-hoc launch path and never touches ConPTY at all, silently producing empty output and rc=0. ALWAYS use an absolute target path when measuring exec behaviour. REMAINING OPEN QUESTION, now properly narrowed: with NO extra flags, choice.exe prints its prompt and then exits 255 in about a second, which is still consistent with the input side reaching EOF -- so step 11's input-lifetime spec may yet be correct, but it must be re-tested with an absolute path and no leaking flags before anyone changes handle code again.

TODO: 2026-07-23 ROOT CAUSE NARROWED -- the child does not read the pipe we write to. Measured after removing every earlier confound (absolute target path, MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1, exec flags no longer leaking into child args): (a) the ConPTY is genuinely attached -- 'exec <abs>cmd.exe /c "mode con"' prints 'Status for device CON: Lines 30, Columns 120' from inside the child; (b) the injection WRITE SUCCEEDS -- after replacing the swallowing 'try { WriteFile(...); } catch { }' with a checked write, no failure is reported, so the bytes really do enter inputWrite; (c) the child nevertheless behaves as though stdin is at EOF from the first instant -- 'cmd /v:on /c "set /p X=P: && echo GOT-!X!"' prints its prompt and returns rc=1 IMMEDIATELY without waiting, choice.exe prints its prompt then exits 255, and injecting LATE (appending to the keystrokes file 4s after the child is up) changes nothing. CR vs LF is not the cause -- 'y\r' behaves exactly like 'y\n'. CONCLUSION: the pseudoconsole is wired for OUTPUT but the child's STDIN is not the pseudoconsole's input side; our writes land in a pipe nobody reads. NEXT INVESTIGATION, narrowest first: confirm what the child's STD_INPUT_HANDLE actually is (a trustworthy instrument this time -- the earlier P/Invoke probe returned ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE even on a known-good console and must be validated against that control BEFORE its readings are believed); check whether the child inherits the PARENT's stdin (wkappbot-core is spawned detached, so its own stdin is NUL/closed, which would produce exactly this instant-EOF); and re-read the CreatePseudoConsole call order -- inputRead is closed at line 142 right after the pseudoconsole is created, which is correct per the docs ONLY if CreatePseudoConsole has already taken it. IMPORTANT: the swallowed-write fix is worth keeping regardless -- it converted a lie ('Injected N bytes') into a checkable fact and is what allowed (b) to be established at all.

TODO: 2026-07-23 THE SIBLING THAT 'WORKS' DOES NOT USE ConPTY AT ALL -- compare before building further. wkstdpty.ps1, cited across this cluster as the working interactive driver, contains NO CreatePseudoConsole: it sets psi.RedirectStandardInput on an ordinary Process and writes via p.StandardInput.Write(text) then closes the stream. So the premise that we have a proven ConPTY input path is FALSE; what is proven is that a plain redirected-stdin pipe drives a target. Re-reading the agy evidence with that in mind: the 99 test's prompt arrived through the '-i <prompt>' COMMAND-LINE argument, not through keystrokes, and the '/quit' that WAS supposed to arrive via the keystrokes file is exactly the thing that never worked (C5 hang, child killed at KillAfterMs). Every apparent keystroke success this session is explained without ConPTY input ever delivering a byte. CONSEQUENCE FOR DESIGN: the T0-T3 ladder should treat plain-pipe stdin as a FIRST-CLASS rung that is known to work, not as a pre-Win10 fallback beneath ConPTY -- today exec only uses the redirected path when ConPTY is unsupported, which is backwards relative to the evidence. NEXT STEP, cheapest decisive experiment: run the same target twice through exec, once forced down the plain-redirect path and once through ConPTY, and compare whether 'set /p' receives an injected byte. If plain-pipe delivers and ConPTY does not, the fix is to route keystroke/reply injection through a redirected stdin (or to dual-wire it) rather than to keep debugging the pseudoconsole input side. Do NOT change handle code before running that comparison -- three rounds were already spent editing ConPTY internals on hypotheses that measurement later killed.

TODO: 2026-07-23 (user directive, SPEC) DELIVERY-CHANNEL LADDER -- deliver input through the channel the target is ACTUALLY connected to, chosen per app, never hardcoded per app name. Today exec picks ConPTY whenever the host supports it and treats a redirected pipe as a pre-Win10 fallback; the evidence says that is backwards, and neither choice serves a legacy GUI app at all. FOUR RUNGS. T0 STATIC CLASSIFY (free, reliable): read the PE subsystem -- CONSOLE vs WINDOWS. A WINDOWS-subsystem target has no stdin to speak of and must NOT be driven by any stdin mechanism; route it to the a11y layer (UIA ValuePattern / focusless type / SendInput) which this repo already has, and say so in the log rather than silently writing bytes nobody reads. T1 PLAIN PIPE (the rung PROVEN to work): RedirectStandardInput on an ordinary Process and write to StandardInput -- this is exactly what wkstdpty does, and it is the only input path in this codebase ever observed to deliver. T2 CONSOLE/ConPTY: for a target that reads the CONSOLE INPUT BUFFER (ReadConsoleInput) rather than the stdin stream -- choice.exe is the canonical example -- a pipe write is invisible to it, so it needs real console input records. T3 CLEAN FAIL: no channel worked; report WHICH rungs were tried and why each was rejected, never a silent no-op. SELECTION MUST BE OBSERVED, NOT GUESSED: whether a console app reads the stream or the console buffer cannot be determined statically, so the ladder ATTEMPTS a rung, watches for a bounded interval for evidence of progress (output advanced / prompt consumed / process exited), and escalates on no-progress. Per-app hardcoding is banned -- that is the whole point of a ladder. NON-NEGOTIABLE OBSERVABILITY, learned the hard way today: every rung logs which channel was chosen and whether the write was CONFIRMED (bytes accepted AND evidence of consumption), because a log line reading 'Injected N bytes' while nothing was delivered is what cost this session most of its measurements. BUILD ORDER: run the T1-vs-T2 comparison from the previous step FIRST (same target, both paths, does set /p receive a byte), then wire T0/T1/T2 selection, then add the GUI/a11y rung last since it crosses into a different subsystem entirely.

NAVIGATION (2026-07-23 tier split): this T1 core holds the CURRENT CONTRACT -- the exec flags (--keys, --onexit, --reply, --reply-max, --noise, --noise-log), the token grammar, the pipeline order, and the DELIVERY-CHANNEL LADDER spec that supersedes the older T0-T3 sketch. The dated investigation history -- two wrong diagnoses that each looked correct, the MSYS path-conversion and shim-hijack confounds that produced them, the argument-leakage bug, the lying injection log, and the wkstdpty finding that no ConPTY input path has ever been shown to deliver a byte -- lives in the single ref tier 'wkexec-conpty-keystrokes-ladder-ref'. READ THAT REF before re-opening any input-delivery question; nearly every plausible hypothesis in this area has already been tried and killed by measurement, and the ref records which measurement killed which. ADD dated entries to the ref, never to this core, and never open a SECOND ref tier -- one cluster in this catalog orphaned a 34-step archive exactly that way, by making a new -t3 sibling and leaving the original linked from nothing.
